item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Mecca Agreement gives Turkey new leverage and risk in equal measure
item.description:
Mecca Agreement gives Turkey new leverage and risk in equal measure

Submitted by Fatma Menal Akın on Tue, 08/25/2026 - 09:04
The collective defence commitment has evoked comparisons with Nato, but the three countries still face major political, operational and technological hurdles
A woman walks past armoured vehicles at the International Defence Industry Fair in Istanbul, 9 May 2017 (Yasin Akgul/AFP)
Off

The defence pact signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known for now as the Mecca Agreement, has laid down a firm statement of political intent: to sharpen regional deterrence, and to put the burden of the region's security back in the hands of the region itself.

Yet the collective defence promise at the heart of the pact raises as many questions as it answers.

Its central clause, that an attack on one member is to be treated as an attack on all, has fuelled expectations that the three countries could build a Nato-style deterrent of their own.

But the structure is still in its infancy, and much remains unclear: how far it will hold up on the ground, how durable the political trust between the parties will prove, and how military, intelligence and technological capabilities are to be pooled.

For Turkey, the timing of the initiative, and the choice of partners, matter every bit as much as the agreement itself.

At a moment when the region's existing deterrents are wearing thin, when Washington's role in Middle Eastern security is being reopened for debate, and when tensions between Israel and Turkey are taking on new dimensions, Ankara appears to be reaching for regional partnerships that widen its own security options.

Speaking to Turkish media after the signing, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the talks between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had been running for more than two years.

Years of instability, the widening theatres of conflict since 7 October 2023 and a security balance in the Red Sea that has come apart have made the search for a regional answer look all the more urgent.

Analysts suggest that what the pact offers Ankara, at least for now, is less a hard military guarantee than fresh diplomatic room to manoeuvre.

It is also expected to deepen Turkey's security ties with Saudi Arabia and to multiply its options across the region.

The flip side is that Ankara now faces the risk of being dragged into crises that are not its own, of stretching its military and industrial capacity past its limits, and of taking on commitments that sit awkwardly with its obligations inside Nato.

New bargaining chip  

The security landscape that produced the agreement is one in which the regional order that the United States has spent years trying to build in the Middle East is under serious strain.

Washington's strategy rested largely on drawing Israel closer to the Gulf states, containing and deterring Iran, and gradually winding down its own direct military footprint in the region.

The Abraham Accords supplied the diplomatic scaffolding for that architecture, and the normalisation deal expected between Saudi Arabia and Israel was meant to be its keystone. 

Mecca Agreement: A Muslim Nato or yet another Baghdad Pact?
Read More »

For Dr Yasir Atan, deputy director at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), what lies behind the pact is the erosion of the region's deterrent mechanisms and a security balance that grows more brittle by the month.

In Atan's reading, Turkey is looking for a new principal partner amid the deepening regional insecurity that followed the 7 October attack by Hamas and the war with Iran.

Building that partnership, however, means holding another balance: between Nato membership, relations with Washington and a security rivalry with Israel that is hardening by the day.

Turkey and Israel, Atan says, increasingly see each other as a threat across a widening set of arenas with Syria, Cyprus, the Eastern Mediterranean and Somalia among them.

Atan sees the United States acting as the referee in that contest, managing the friction between Turkey and Israel.

The partnership with Riyadh and Islamabad, he argues, could strengthen Ankara's hand and its bargaining power in Washington, while making it harder for Israel to isolate Turkey there.

That approach dovetails with the argument Ankara has been making for years: that the region should own its own security.

But Turkey's aim is probably less to step into America's shoes than to build relationships that keep Washington's Israel-centred policies from leaving it out in the cold.

Dr Betul Dogan-Akkas, who works on Gulf politics and regional security as deputy director of Ankara University's centre for Middle Eastern Studies and a faculty member in its international relations department, does not expect any of the three countries to strike out entirely on their own from Washington.

But she says the Israel-centred cast of US policy is pushing regional powers to work more closely with one another.

Why Riyadh and Islamabad?  

Ankara's turn towards a new regional security arrangement matters, but so does the question of why Riyadh and Islamabad, of all capitals, emerged as the partners of choice.

Turkey's search for new avenues of cooperation against the region's uncertainties, without tearing up the alliances it already has, brought the three countries into the same security equation. 

Why the Mecca Agreement has given the UAE-Israel alliance the jitters
Read More »

For Atan, that choice is bound up with how the region's security environment has shifted in recent years. A United States inclined to pare back its commitments in the Middle East, the deepening insecurity since 7 October and the new equation thrown up by the war with Iran have all pushed Turkey to look for fresh partners.

Saudi Arabia, Atan says, is seen in Ankara as a "principal partner", both for its weight in the Gulf and for the reach of its ties elsewhere in the region.

Pakistan emerges as the third leg of the structure thanks to its long-running military and defence relationship with Turkey and the security bonds it already maintains with Riyadh.

In Atan's view, Turkey read the partnership as an opportunity within the new regional equation that took shape after the war with Iran. Whether the trio will widen its circle, though, is a matter of some disagreement.

One of the candidates Atan points to is Egypt. Bringing Cairo in at a later stage, he suggests, could help turn the three-way partnership into something closer to a broader regional security framework.

Egypt's inclusion would stretch the structure's geographic reach along both the Eastern Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

Akkas is more cautious. Egypt may be among the first names raised whenever expansion comes up, she says, but "given its military structure and the security problems it would generate, it isn't actually the most rational partner".

Undefined edges  

Because the trust between the parties has yet to be tested in the field, the limits of the security backing they could actually offer one another remain unclear.

Fidan's remarks suggest the parties are alive to the operational and political difficulties ahead. But for all the preparation and planning, the fact that strategic trust between the three, and their capacity to act as one, has never been put to the test is among the pact's biggest unknowns.

For Akkas, the real question is how much room the domestic politics of the three countries will leave for a long-term partnership. 

'Playing with fire': Israel's Syria strike tests Turkey after Mecca defence pact
Read More »

The balance of political forces in Pakistan, whether Mohammed bin Salman ascends to the Saudi throne, and elections in Turkey are all, she notes, processes capable of testing the political will behind the arrangement.

Atan, for his part, stresses that trust of this kind has to be proven over time, and that the limits of the security support the three could extend to one another have yet to come into focus.

For all the talk of security, the pact identifies no adversary and offers no definition of the threat it exists to counter.

What it does offer is a window onto Ankara's thinking; a deterrent posture, aimed at heading off dangers before they materialise.

That leaves an obvious question hanging: in the event of an actual attack, what would trigger the commitment, and how would it work?

Akkas draws attention to Fidan's choice of words: he spoke of a "common threat" rather than a common enemy.

"Naming an enemy points to a more aggressive posture," she says, "whereas drawing the boundaries of a threat describes an approach built around defence and deterrence."

Once that common threat is defined, she argues, it will become clearer who the pact is meant to protect and when it would be activated.

At this stage, she stresses, the agreement is not concerned with the small-scale attacks the region contends with day to day.

Layered regional equation   

Managing the new partnership, though, leaves Turkey with a set of diplomatic sensitivities and risks to navigate.

Ankara has to keep its channels open with Iran, contain the scale of its confrontation with Israel, handle a delicate relationship with the UAE and meet Saudi expectations on security, all at once. 

Not least because one reading now circulating in public debate holds that the pact amounts to a Sunni security axis aimed at Iran.

Fidan insists the agreement is not an offensive structure directed at any country, and that its purpose is to shore up regional stability and build mutual security and solidarity among the parties.

Is the Mecca Agreement Israel's worst nightmare come true?
Read More »

As he frames it, the alliance is less about targeting an outside actor than about members underwriting one another's security. Iran, he underlines, is not in its sights. 

Atan, too, argues against reading the pact as a sectarian bloc. What drives the region, in his view, is not sectarian dynamics but the national security calculations of the actors involved, their real capabilities and the geopolitics binding them together.

Seen in that light, the agreement reflects more than a mutual search for security among its signatories. It also captures Ankara's bid to take on a more active security role at a moment of deep regional uncertainty.

Even with the insistence that no country is being targeted, how this new security convergence is read against the region's existing balance of power remains a live question for Ankara.

Iran, in particular, is one of the actors Turkey both diverges from on regional files and works with, keeping diplomatic channels running throughout.

That leaves Ankara having to weigh the delicate balances in its relationship with Tehran as it develops the new partnership.

Akkas, though, says the parties will need to persuade Tehran that the agreement is not aimed at it.

With Israel and Iran locked in confrontation, that will be no easy task, and it stands as one of the Mecca Agreement's more serious tests.

Nor is Iran the only balance Ankara has to hold. As it builds the new security partnership, it must simultaneously manage its existing relationships inside the Gulf and the differing security outlooks it finds there.

Akkas points out that as Turkey deepens security cooperation with Saudi Arabia, it also has to preserve the equilibrium it has built with the UAE.

Abu Dhabi's purchase of an air defence system from Israel, she notes, has made the question of what constitutes a shared threat in the Gulf, and how security is perceived there, considerably more tangled.

Military planning and cooperation matter, she says, but so does the pact's diplomatic language, and the way it is explained to Western allies.

First test   

Where the limits of this security commitment are drawn may well be settled by Saudi Arabia's own security and by the Red Sea-Bab al-Mandeb corridor, which looms as a proving ground.

A fresh crisis along that stretch of water could quickly become a shared security problem for the signatories. 

Any disruption to maritime trade there would land not only on Riyadh, but directly on the security calculations of Turkey, which has both commercial and strategic interests running through the Red Sea.

How the Mecca Agreement aims to manage US separation from Middle East
Read More »

Should Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalate again, Atan says, the question of what exactly Turkey's commitment amounts to under the agreement would come to the fore, and that ambiguity is a test in its own right.

He stresses that the Houthis fight in a decentralised, fragmented fashion.

In a threat of that kind, he predicts, the classic security scenario of squaring off against a conventional actor simply would not apply and that, in itself, is a problem in waiting.

A similar tension surfaces in Yemen. Akkas notes that if Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia flare up again, Ankara will want to honour the security commitment it has made to Riyadh while keeping clear of becoming a direct party to Yemen's chronic conflict.

Sending a message of deterrence is one thing. Being obliged to send troops when deterrence fails is quite another.

The pact's real credibility, Atan says, will only become visible when a crisis of that sort actually arrives.

As Akkas puts it, how the common threat is defined will determine "in what circumstances, and for whom, the pact would be activated".

For Turkey, the deeper worry is being pulled into a new and open-ended military front in a theatre that poses it no direct threat.

Systems mismatch

Militarily and industrially, whether the pact can match its political ambition in the field depends on how far the parties can make their existing capabilities and systems work together.

Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence analyst and chief executive of Mergen Analytical Strategies, says the relationship between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan has already moved beyond a conventional buyer-seller arrangement, but has yet to reach the level of a genuine multinational consortium along the lines of Eurofighter. 

Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt's inclusion in Mecca agreement, sources say
Read More »

The most realistic model, at least to begin with, would be a Turkish-led programme architecture with Saudi and Pakistani industrial work packages settled by negotiation, Mevlutoglu says.

Turkey would bring the largest body of platform design and systems engineering know-how; Pakistan its engineering, integration and production experience; Saudi Arabia capital, procurement scale and industrial capacity. Repeated cooperation over time, he adds, could grow into something closer to a genuine consortium. 

But shared ownership of technology is another matter: source codes, mission-system architecture, propulsion technology, radar algorithms, electronic warfare libraries and the division of export rights are among the far thornier issues standing between the three and genuine joint production.

Mevlutoglu would not measure the agreement's success by whether it turns into a "Middle Eastern Nato".

A more realistic architecture, he says, would combine strategic consultation, intelligence sharing, exercises, contingency planning, missile warning, air and maritime surveillance, industrial cooperation, and military support packages agreed in advance for specific crisis scenarios. 

In air defence especially, he suggests a federated model would be the more workable route: each country keeping its own sovereign network, with certain data and early-warning feeds shared across controlled links. 

Operational risks

One of the biggest technical hurdles to the pact is the mismatch between the weapons and command systems the three countries use.

On paper, Turkey's platform development capacity, Pakistan's experience in fighter production and integration, and Saudi financial power fit neatly together. 

But finding the money is not the same thing as speeding the programme up.

Mecca agreement: Why Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan teamed up
Read More »

Turkey's military infrastructure is built to Nato standards. Saudi Arabia relies largely on American and other Western systems. Pakistan's inventory is a patchwork of American, European, Chinese and domestically produced equipment.

Past a certain point, Mevlutoglu says, it is engineering integration that sets the critical path, and everything turns on the shape Saudi participation takes.  

The three countries have the potential to build a broader industrial base between them, he says, but full independence in fighter jet engines, advanced microelectronics and specialist materials is likely to take a decade or longer. 

Turning political will into a functioning security mechanism depends on clearing away the ambiguities that remain, and on establishing how far the parties can actually act together on technology and intelligence sharing, training, exercises, defence industry and finance.

The agreement's true limits, though, will only emerge in the face of shifting regional threats, and above all in how the three behave during the first serious crisis or attack.

Whether the Mecca Agreement can become something more than a political declaration will, in large part, be answered there.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel versus the UN: How it got this bad
item.description:
Israel versus the UN: How it got this bad

Submitted by Daniel Tester on Thu, 07/16/2026 - 13:18
Amid the genocide in Gaza, already tense relations between the United Nations and Israel have reached a new low
A Palestinian boy holds a sack of flour at a United Nations Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa) aid distribution centre in Gaza City in April 2013 (AFP)
On

Israeli forces seized the last remaining facility run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa, in occupied East Jerusalem on Tuesday.

It’s but the latest fallout in the acrimonious relationship between Israel and the global organisation, which Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and fellow politicians have said is biased against their country. 

In recent years, Israel has quit some of the UN’s dozens of bodies, offices, departments and specialised agencies.

It doesn’t do so alone, often coordinating the moves with the US during the first and second administrations of President Donald Trump.

Search for the terms "Israel" and "UN" on Google and among the top results is a sponsored page, paid for by the government of Israel and entitled "UN bias against Israel". 

There is even an Israel-linked organisation called "UN Watch" founded to scrutinise alleged antisemitism across the UN's various arms. 

Israeli and US withdrawals have hurt UN agencies, which depend on funds from member states to support those in need on the ground.

Below, Middle East Eye explains how the relationship has deteriorated and from which agencies Israel has withdrawn.

How are relations between the UN and Israel?

Israel has sat at the UN General Assembly since it became a full member under UN Resolution 273 in 1949, a year after the creation of the state. But it’s never been elected as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council, despite seeking a seat. 

Relations have long been tense: the phrase “Um-Shmum”, popularised by Israel's founding Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion in the 1950s, is a Hebrew sign of contempt towards the UN.

The UN has mediated in several Arab-Israeli conflicts, including the 1967 Arab-Israeli war via Security Council Resolution 242, and the 1973 war via Resolutions 338-340. 

And in 1975, the General Assembly passed Resolution 3379, which stated that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”. This was met with fury from Israel and the US, and repealed in 1991 to incentivise Israel to participate in the Madrid Conference talks.

In 1978, the UN established the Unifil peacekeeping mission in Lebanon following Israel's invasion of its northern neighbour. 

Palestine gained observer status at the UN in 2012 after a decades-long campaign - but the US and Israel prevented full membership.

Resolution 2334, passed by the Security Council in 2016, declared as illegal all Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territories occupied since 1967, re-enforced by an International Court of Justice ruling in 2024. Israel called the resolution “shameful” and retaliated by cutting aid to Senegal, which had backed the resolution as a non-permanent Security Council member. 

How Israel quit Unesco

Israeli moves against UN agencies have increased in the past two decades and only accelerated amid its genocide in Gaza.

The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) promotes and protects science and culture. It has had tensions with Israel since it admitted Palestine in 2011, prompting Israel and the US to pull funding. 

Israel was further angered in 2017 when Unesco designated the Ibrahimi Mosque in the occupied West Bank as an endangered World Heritage Site belonging to the State of Palestine.

Israel officially quit in 2019, alleging that Unesco had been “manipulated by Israel’s enemies and continually singles out the Jewish state for condemnation”.

The US, which funded 20 percent of Unesco’s budget, quit during Trump’s first administration in 2017, citing its “anti-Israel bias”.

Washington rejoined in October 2023 under President Joe Biden, before quitting again in July 2025 during the second Trump presidency. 

Israel bulldozes Unrwa

Unrwa (the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East) is the largest humanitarian aid organisation in Gaza and the West Bank.

Overseeing facilities including schools, shelters and emergency kitchens, it was founded in 1949 to support the estimated 700,000 Palestinian refugees displaced by the 1948 Nakba.

Israel opposes Unwra because the agency considers Palestinians to be refugees, implying they have a right to return to their lands seized by Israel.

It cut ties with the agency in January 2025 after declaring it a terrorist group and banning it from Israel and occupied Palestine. David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli government, said “Unrwa is riddled with Hamas operatives” and that “if a state funds Unrwa, that state is funding terrorists”.

The move came after Israel said in January 2024 that some of Unrwa’s 11,000 Gaza staff were involved in the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, during which more than 1,100 Israelis were killed.

In April 2024, the independent Colonna report found that Unrwa had ensured that it was politically neutral. Unrwa sacked nine staff in August 2024 after a UN investigation found possible evidence of involvement.  

Without Unrwa, Israel renewed its blockade on aid coming into Gaza in March 2025, which eventually led to the declaration of famine in Gaza in August 2025. It has killed 391 Unrwa staff members during its genocide in Gaza.

Israel’s ban on Unrwa was condemned, and ruled as unlawful in an advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice in October 2025, which also found that Israel has not substantiated its allegations. 

In January, Israel bulldozed Unrwa’s HQ in occupied East Jerusalem, weeks after passing legislation to cut off the agency's water and electricity. The demolition was led by far-right Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir.

Phillippe Lazzarini, the outgoing commissioner-general of Unrwa, told Middle East Eye’s David Hearst Podcast in April that “the dismantlement of the agency has become an [Israeli] objective” and that “the campaign against the agency is politically driven”, despite using “a pretext of a total infiltration by Hamas into the organisation”.

Israel leaves the UNHRC

The UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC), based in Geneva, is designated with protecting human rights, alongside the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Israel has never been elected as a member.

In February 2025, Israel cut ties, accusing the UNHRC of “ongoing and unrelenting institutional bias against Israel”. The US quit the previous day. 

The UNHRC had criticised Israel’s genocide in Gaza, adopting a resolution in April 2024 demanding it end its blockade and “all other forms of collective punishment”.

Meirav Eilon Shahar, Israel’s then UN representative, stormed out in protest at the resolution, which the Israeli government said “provides legitimacy for Palestinian 'resistance' to the 'occupation'”.

Israel, the US and many western nations had long opposed the council’s standing Agenda Item 7, introduced in 2006, to ensure an annual debate on the “Human Rights Situation in Palestine and Other Occupied Arab Territories” - the UNHRC’s only permanent country-specific agenda item. 

The US quit in 2018, citing anti-Israel bias, before rejoining in 2021 under President Biden. 

Israel and other UN agencies

The US announced in January 2026 that it would cut ties with 66 international organisations, 31 of which were UN entities. Israel followed days later, formally announcing that it had cut ties with the following six organisations: 

UN Women: The UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women is the UN agency that advocates for women, girls and LGBT people. Israel said it had “deliberately ignored all cases of sexual violence committed against Israeli women on Oct. 7th, 2023”. But the agency had issued multiple statements condemning the Hamas-led attacks. 

Unctad: Part of the UN Secretariat focused on economic issues, the UN Conference for Trade and Development published reports about the economic price of the occupation of Palestine, which Israel described as “virulent anti-Israel reports”.

The UN Alliance of Civilizations: Founded by then UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan in 2005, it aims to foster “intercultural dialogue, understanding and cooperation”. Israel said it had “severed ties”, before subsequently saying it had not been invited to join, adding that the Alliance “has instead for years been used as a platform for attacks against Israel”.

UN Energy: This group coordinates energy policy in line with the Paris Agreement climate goals. The Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs described it as a “wasteful organisation” that “reflects the excessive and inefficient bureaucracy of the UN”.

The Global Forum on Migration and Development: This is an annual intergovernmental forum previously attended by all UN member states, founded by Annan. Israel said it “erodes the ability of sovereign nations to enforce their own immigration laws”. The forum has no power to make binding decisions.

The Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children in Armed Conflict: A UN-appointed expert who reports on the rights of children affected by war, the role is currently held by Maltese diplomat Vanessa Frazier. In June 2024, her predecessor, Argentinian diplomat Virginia Gamba, added Israel to the UN blacklist of warring parties committing rights violations against children. Israel complained that it was “the only democratic country to be listed, alongside Isis and Boko Haram”.

UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia: Israel never joined the Mena regional bloc, which consists of 21 Muslim-majority member states, and instead joined its Western European counterpart. The Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that it had “severed ties with” the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia, having been “disengaged for years”, adding: “The organization issues virulent anti-Israel reports annually, and serves as a basis for further anti-Israel resolutions.” 

Could Israel quit other agencies?

Israel has not quit all UN agencies - but some are in its sights.

Israeli critics of the UN have encouraged it to sever ties with Ocha (the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs), which oversees UN humanitarian relief in natural disaster zones and warzones such as Gaza. Its situation reports are cited by journalists, NGOs and academics worldwide. In July 2025, Israel refused to renew the visa for Jonathan Whittall, Ocha’s top official in occupied Palestine, citing “biased and hostile conduct”.   

Others in Israel want it to quit the WHO (World Health Organization), which the US, the organisation’s largest donor, left in January. Israel is still a member.

Limor Son Har Melech, the far-right Israeli lawmaker who chairs the Knesset’s health committee, said in January: “The World Health Organization has long since ceased to operate as a professional and objective organization.”   

Senior Israeli officials also say it should ignore rulings from the ICJ (International Court of Justice), the UN’s main court, to which all members are automatically a party.

In January 2024, the ICJ ruled that Israel must take “all measures within its power” to prevent genocide. Ben Gvir said: “The ruling of the antisemitic court in The Hague confirms what was already known: this court does not seek justice but rather the persecution of the Jewish people.”

Israel and the UN secretary-general

Israel cut ties with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on 28 May after his office formally named Israel, in an annual report, as a state credibly suspected of sexual violence.

The declaration followed multiple reports by human rights organisations and media outlets, including Middle East Eye, documenting allegations of rape and other sexual violence by Israeli forces against Palestinians.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry said in a 28 May statement that the decision was “shameful and absurd” and “further proof of the UN’s true nature: a politicized and corrupt organization that has abandoned its founding principles and systematically targets Israel as its primary mission”.

Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for Guterres, said Israel’s announcement was “more symbolic than anything”, and that the UN would continue to work with the Israeli mission. Guterres’ 10-year term ends in December. 

Israel had previously declared Guterres a “persona non grata” in October 2024, banning him from entering Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories. 

Israel Katz, then Israeli foreign minister, said Guterres was an “anti-Israel secretary-general”, and claimed he had not condemned Iran’s attacks on Israel in October 2024 (Guterres had condemned the conflict as well as previous attacks on Israel, and confirmed that he condemned Iran’s attacks after the Israeli announcement).

For any country, cutting ties with the UN secretary-general is a highly unusual move. The last such case was when the USSR and China blacklisted Trygve Lie, the UN's first secretary-general, in the 1950s. 

In 2016, Netanyahu accused Guterres’ predecessor, Ban Ki-moon, of “encouraging terror” after he said that Palestinian attacks were the result of decades of Israeli occupation. 

Israel rejects special rapporteur

The UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories is appointed by the UNHRC to independently report on human rights violations in occupied Palestine.

The current incumbent, Italian legal scholar Francesca Albanese, has criticised Israel since her appointment in 2022 and has been banned from the country, as well as Gaza and the West Bank, since December 2024. 

The Israeli foreign ministry said it was because Albanese observed that “the victims of the October 7 massacre were not murdered because of their Jewishness, but in response to Israeli oppression”.

Israel rejects the work of special rapporteurs. Albanese’s predecessors, including Canadian academic Michael Lynk and the American legal scholar Richard Falk, were also blocked, instead working from neighbouring Jordan. 

In a historic first, Albanese was sanctioned by the US in July 2025 after she urged the ICC to prosecute corporate executives of more than 60 companies, some American, for alleged complicity in Israeli crimes in Gaza. 

The sanctions were lifted by a US judge on 21 May before being reimposed six days later.

Mecca Agreement gives Turkey new leverage and risk in equal measure

The defence pact signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known for now as the Mecca Agreement, has laid down a firm statement of political intent: to sharpen regional deterrence, and to put the burden of the region's security back in the hands of the region itself.

Yet the collective defence promise at the heart of the pact raises as many questions as it answers.

Its central clause, that an attack on one member is to be treated as an attack on all, has fuelled expectations that the three countries could build a Nato-style deterrent of their own.

But the structure is still in its infancy, and much remains unclear: how far it will hold up on the ground, how durable the political trust between the parties will prove, and how military, intelligence and technological capabilities are to be pooled.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How football's governing bodies support illegal Israeli settlement clubs
item.description:
How football's governing bodies support illegal Israeli settlement clubs

Submitted by Mahmoud Elsobky on Tue, 08/25/2026 - 13:25
While Palestinian facilities are either destroyed or crippled by Israeli checkpoints, Fifa and Uefa are continuing to prop up Israeli settlement teams
Israeli players from the Ironi Ariel football club attend a training session at their stadium in the illegal Israeli settlement of Ariel in the occupied West Bank on 21 September 2016 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off

Football in the occupied West Bank has been brought to a near standstill since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza.

Palestinian players struggle to reach training grounds, matches are routinely cancelled because of checkpoints and military closures, and hundreds of sports facilities have either been damaged or destroyed.

But in illegal Israeli settlements, Israeli football teams are thriving, with players continuing to train and compete while clubs expand their facilities.

An investigation by Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ) and Bridges Investigations for Middle East Eye has found that illegal settlement-based clubs are participating in Israeli domestic competitions with the backing of the Israel Football Association (IFA), while Fifa and Uefa continue to recognise and financially support the IFA.

According to the investigation, Fifa, which formally says it is committed to respecting internationally recognised human rights through its statutes and strategic goals, has not only declined to take action against settlement clubs; its Fifa+ platform also broadcasts their matches.

For Palestinian players, the consequences have been felt every time they try to train or travel to a match.

Mahdi al-Assi, a goalkeeper for the Palestinian youth team, knows this well. 

Getting to the pitch can mean hours spent at checkpoints, while training itself can be disrupted by raids and teargas, he says.

"More than once, I've set off three or four hours before training, only for them [Israeli soldiers] to turn us back at the checkpoint for no reason at all," he told MEE.

Meanwhile, just a few kilometres from where al-Assi plays, the floodlights are on at a football pitch inside the Israeli settlement of Givat Ze'ev. 

Here, the Beitar Givat Ze'ev team trains on land that international law classifies as occupied Palestinian territory.

A journey of checkpoints and closures

Al-Assi said that routine travel between Palestinian cities has become a gruelling ordeal because of Israeli military checkpoints.

Restrictions have grown since Israel's last elections in 2022, and since October 2023, when Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza.

According to al-Assi, Israeli forces also disrupt sporting activities by storming pitches.

Since Israel launched its war on Gaza, 292 sports facilities have been completely or partially destroyed in the besieged enclave and the occupied West Bank, according to data obtained from the Palestinian Football Association.

The association's league has also been suspended.

'We can't schedule the league, the gates could be shut at the time of a match'

– Susan Shalabi, Palestinian Football Association

"It became too dangerous to keep the league going," said Susan Shalabi, vice-president of the Palestinian Football Association. 

"There are more and more checkpoints, and towns are sealed off by electronic gates, trapping people inside."

According to Shalabi, it has become virtually impossible to arrange matches: "We can't schedule the league; the gates could be shut at the time of a match, so it gets cancelled."

According to al-Assi, after the league was cancelled he was no longer able to train regularly, so he turned to a private coach.

"Because of the war, there are no games being played now. But playing matches is a basic element in a footballer’s development, so I’m training with a private coach."

This poses an additional financial burden, but he remains determined to continue playing, in the hope of representing his country in international competitions.

Football and settlement expansion

The situation is markedly different for clubs operating in the hundreds of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The settlement of Ariel was established in 1978 on land Israel seized from Palestinians in the area of Salfit. Last year, the mayor of Ariel, Yair Shatbon, launched a long-term plan to allocate a large budget to the development of the sports sector. This included a new stadium on Efrata Street and more football pitches and sports facilities throughout the settlement.

Why does Fifa refuse to sanction Israel?
Read More »

Shatbon also announced a project to modernise the main pitch of FC Ironi Ariel, including replacing the turf with artificial grass that meets Fifa standards.

According to Shalabi, the issue of settlement clubs dates back to 2013, when their details appeared on the official website of the IFA, before later being removed as international attention grew.

"Fifa didn't take any position on clubs, so their numbers went from five to around nine today," she said. "Fifa just tells you to go back to the UN, and what does the UN say? It says these are occupied territories," she said.

Ironi Ariel is one of nine football clubs associated with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Some play directly within settlements, while others are based there or use their facilities.

A 2016 report by Human Rights Watch criticised Fifa for funding matches held within settlements, describing them as "illegal under international humanitarian law".

Article 49, paragraph 6 of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War states: "The Occupying Power shall not deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies.”

Broadcasting matches

The relationship between Fifa and settlement football extends beyond the IFA's participation in domestic competitions. 

Fifa+ has also carried matches played at a ground in occupied East Jerusalem. On 1 June 2026, Inside World Football reported that Fifa+ had broadcast and archived matches from the Har Homa settlement and shared links to them on DAZN.

The broadcasts took place while the participation of settlement clubs in Israeli competitions was being challenged at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The Israel Youth League page on Fifa+ includes replays of Nordia Jerusalem matches played at the Har Homa ground. The IFA's page on the platform also features live matches and replays from its competitions, including matches played at the same ground.

Legal experts tell Fifa Israel is breaking international law as it considers sanctions
Read More »

DAZN says it provides Fifa+ content on demand and describes itself as "the new home of Fifa+".

According to the advocacy group Scottish Sport for Palestine, Fifa+ generates revenue through advertising and sponsorship, as well as commercial expansion and an increasing audience base.

Matches involving clubs linked to settlements may therefore bring revenue to Fifa while providing a platform for showcasing the clubs and their players.

Fifa's budgets consolidate financial data in a way that makes it difficult to track revenue generated by its digital platforms. Revenue from digital broadcasting is consolidated within the federation's overall budget, which stands at nearly $13bn for the current financial cycle, 2023-2026.

The budget shows that television broadcasting revenue alone amounted to $3.092bn from matches in 2026.

MEE reached out to Fifa for comment but did not receive a response by time of publication.

Fifa declines to act

In March 2026, Fifa's Disciplinary Committee responded to a complaint by the Palestinian Football Association over the participation of settlement clubs in the Israeli league. 

The complaint had been submitted during the 74th Fifa Congress in May 2024.

The committee said it would not take any action against the clubs because of what it described as “the unresolved legal status of the West Bank under public international law".

It did, however, fine the IFA 150,000 Swiss francs ($190,000) for "committing grave and systematic abuses relating to discrimination and racism; tolerance of politicised and militaristic messages; and exclusion of Palestinians from sports infrastructure in the West Bank".

Steve Cockburn, the head of Economic and Social Justice at Amnesty International, described Fifa's decision as "a failure to enforce Fifa's own rules". 

'Fifa had a clear opportunity to both defend the rights of Palestinians and uphold international law. But… it has shamefully chosen to abandon both'

– Steve Cockburn, Amnesty International

"The decision is also a flagrant violation of international law. Fifa had a clear opportunity to both defend the rights of Palestinians and uphold international law. But by taking this decision, it has shamefully chosen to abandon both," he said.

"The International Court of Justice has stated quite clearly that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful, and that settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory are illegal," he added.

Amnesty wrote to both Fifa and Uefa on 1 October 2025, more than a week before the so-called ceasefire took hold in Gaza, and called on them to suspend the IFA from their competitions until clubs based in illegal settlements on occupied Palestinian land are barred from the Israeli football leagues.

Omar Shaker, who handled the Occupied Territories and Israel at Human Rights Watch before resigning in February, said: "Some of the land on which these stadiums are built is owned by families of players who can't get into them or play there."

Shaker pointed out that Fifa's regulations are clear: "You cannot play matches on the territory of any member state without obtaining its explicit permission."

Sajed Karakra, the coach of the Palestinian Under-20 national team, echoed this view and said he saw the participation of settlement clubs in the Israeli league as part of a wider policy.

"The participation of these sports teams is aimed at strengthening and supporting settlements," he said.

Karakra also condemned the paralysis of the sports system in the West Bank.

He said the contrast between the state of the game before and after 7 October 2023 points to an undeclared strategy to undermine local football and deprive Palestinian players of the physical and technical preparation they need.

Before the war, Karakra said, between 70 and 80 percent of regular sporting activity went ahead despite restrictions, and the Palestinian Football Association successfully ran a regular league under the auspices of the Asian and international federations.

Sports infrastructure in illegal settlements

ARIJ's investigation also found that sports infrastructure in settlements has expanded through projects supported by Mifal HaPais, the Israeli National Lottery.

An active member of both European Lotteries (EL) and the World Lottery Association (WLA), Mifal HaPais' board includes mayors, Likud Party leadership figures and members of settlement councils.

'The building of Israeli settlements in the occupied territories constitutes a war crime'

– Michael Lynk, former UN special rapporteur on Palestine

The current chairman is Itzik Larry, a former chief executive of Toto, the body which handles sports betting in Israel. Other figures involved in its management include Haim Bibas, the mayor of Modiin-Maccabim-Re'ut, and Benjamin Biton, the mayor of Dimona.

Mifal HaPais declares that it is owned by local authorities. Its governance page states that local government figures hold positions within its management structure, and that the mayor of Ma'ale Adumim, Benny Kashriel, was a member of its board.

Data published by the foundation shows that about 46 percent of lottery profits go directly to local authorities, without distinguishing between those in Israel and those in settlements. Mifal HaPais also invests 51 percent of its profits in building and developing sports facilities.

One major project funded by Mifal HaPais was the Sababa Sports Centre in the settlement of Efrat, which includes a near-Olympic-size swimming pool.

According to Mifal HaPais, the centre opened on 14 January 2026, as part of a partnership with the Efrat Settlement Council.

Official data shows that the project received 15.7 million shekels ($5.234m) in direct investment from Mifal HaPais for sports infrastructure. An additional three million shekels ($1m) came in a grant earmarked to cover the deficit and support operations, according to the minutes of the Efrat council for February 2026.

MEE reached out to Mifal HaPais, the EL and the WLA for comment but did not receive a response by time of publication.

European football funding

Settlement clubs continue to participate in the Israeli league, even though their official addresses place them in occupied Palestinian territory.

The IFA, meanwhile, continues to receive funding from both Fifa and Uefa as a member of the two governing bodies.

Human Rights Watch reported in 2016 that, based on financial records, Fifa and Uefa had transferred millions of shekels annually to the IFA. The report argued that by allowing the IFA to stage matches in Israeli settlements, Fifa was engaging in commercial activity that supported those settlements, despite its stated human rights commitments.

That financial relationship has continued. According to an Amnesty International report published in March 2026, both Fifa and Uefa continued to provide funding to the IFA after Israel launched its war on Gaza in 2023.

One of the main funding mechanisms is Uefa's HatTrick programme, which redistributes more than half of the net revenues from the European football championships among its member national associations.

Why one of Europe's most famous football clubs chose to stand with Palestine
Read More »

Funding is divided into three streams: investment funding, given as a one-off grant of up to €5m to each association for strategic projects; annual solidarity payments of around €1m to cover operating costs; and annual incentives of up to €2m to encourage implementation of Uefa programmes.

These include women's football programmes and training, referee development, youth programmes and governance.

Funds are paid to national associations, such as the IFA, rather than directly to individual clubs or local projects.

Uefa's allocations and funding to the IFA under the HatTrick programme between 2024 and 2028 totalled €17m ($17.3m), a 21 percent increase on the previous funding cycle.

Each national association that is a member of Uefa receives the same amount.

The UEFA Foundation for Children, chaired by Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin, also financed the Neighbourhood League project, implemented by Hapoel Katamon Jerusalem or its supporters' association, Katamon Madunim Ohadim. According to the foundation's website, it gave around €320,000 (approximately $370,000) to the project between 2020 and 2023.

At the same time, Hapoel matches were being held in Israeli settlements until 2025, and the association that received the funding is registered at an address in the Har Adar settlement.

MEE reached out to Uefa and the European Union for comment but did not receive a response by time of publication.

From Ma'ale Adumim to Madrid

The relationship between European football and settlement clubs extends beyond funding.

In March 2023, Spanish football organisations and the Spanish Football Federation hosted a delegation from Beitar Ma’ale Adumim, a club based in the Ma'ale Adumim settlement in the occupied West Bank.

The delegation visited La Liga's headquarters and Atletico Madrid's facilities, as well as Spanish clubs and sporting organisations including Getafe and Rayo Vallecano.

The director of Beitar Ma'ale Adumim, Osnat Kaduri, said Atletico Madrid had hosted the delegation and officials from La Liga had accompanied them throughout the visit.

According to Scottish Sport for Palestine, the visit integrated a club operating within an Israeli settlement into European football activities and institutions despite its location in territory considered occupied under international law.

The visit came months after Fifa and Uefa suspended Russian clubs from competitions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Michael Lynk, a former UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territories, describes the difference as "double standards".

"There is no fundamental difference between Russia's illegal invasion and Israel’s ongoing 58-year-long effort to occupy and annex the Palestinian territories," he said.

The European Commission says Israeli settlements are illegal under international law and constitute a major obstacle to peace and the two-state solution.

EU member states are committed to not recognising changes to the 1967 borders, including in Jerusalem, and to ensuring their bilateral agreements with Israel do not apply to the settlements.

Lynk maintains that "the building of Israeli settlements in the occupied territories constitutes a war crime".

This conclusion, he said, is based on the 1998 Rome Statute and repeated resolutions issued by the UN Security Council, General Assembly and Human Rights Council.

Consequently, Lynk says football clubs in these settlements "are an extension of this practice, which is illegal under international law and even under Fifa’s own regulations".

Political pressure grows

Political pressure is also growing against international sporting bodies. 

At an Irish parliamentary session on 9 June, MPs called for Israel to be suspended from international sporting organisations, citing its continued violations and the presence of at least 10 Israeli clubs in the occupied Palestinian territories.

'I try to train and I push myself, despite the circumstances'

– Mahdi al-Assi, goalkeeper for the Palestinian youth team

Sporting bodies have often argued that "sport must remain separate from politics". But Lynk rejects that position.

"Sport is big business," he said. "To say that sport is separate from politics flies in the face of what’s happened in sport over the last 45 years."

James Dorsey, a researcher in international football policy, similarly describes sport and politics as "inseparable twins". 

Mark Doidge, an academic and researcher in the sociology of sport, also rejects the principle of neutrality invoked by Fifa and Uefa when faced with political disputes. "Neutrality is never neutral. It always goes along with the powerful," he said.

While the debate over the role of international sporting bodies continues, settlement sports infrastructure is expanding. 

Between December 2025 and February 2026, the Israeli government approved construction of a corridor linking the Ma’ale Adumim settlement to East Jerusalem. The area is home to three settlement clubs affiliated with the IFA: Beitar Ma’ale Adumim, Beitar Givat Ze’ev and Ironi Yehuda.

The plan reflects a position expressed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has said that the expansion of Ma’ale Adumim reinforces his conviction that “there will never be a Palestinian state”.

For Al-Assi, however, the focus remains on continuing to train and play despite the restrictions.

"I try to train and I push myself, despite the circumstances," he said. "They can't easily stand in our way."

The cover of a children’s book that is to be released by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir (Jewish Power party)

Israel’s far-right Jewish Power party is preparing to release a children’s book celebrating the “activities and achievements” of its leader, National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.

The party is planning to distribute the book to students outside educational institutions in order to target a key and expanding part of Ben Gvir’s electoral base: young Israelis.

Israeli media said the party printed the book “in accessible language adapted for children”.

Titled The Minister Who Didn’t Stop, the book will be launched at the party’s conference in Netanya on 1 September, coinciding with the start of the Israeli school year.

Ben Gvir’s office said: “We are proud to launch the children's book … and through it tell the children of Israel and the entire Israeli people the story of Minister Ben Gvir's tremendous achievements throughout his four years as minister of national security.”

Support for Ben Gvir and Israel’s far right has grown sharply among young Jewish Israelis in recent years.

His younger supporters have greeted him at rallies with the anti-Palestinian chant “Your village should burn”, a chant that celebrates the destruction of Palestinian villages and seeks to drive Palestinians from their homes.

Research published by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 73 percent of Jewish Israelis aged 18 to 24 identified as right-wing, providing fertile ground for politicians such as Ben Gvir.

Some of Ben Gvir’s “tremendous achievements”, however, include becoming an international pariah.

At least 10 countries have barred him from entering over his record as a minister, while a Schengen listing has effectively shut him out of much of Europe.

His international isolation has also come to symbolise Israel’s broader pariah status, which it has earned through its genocide in Gaza and apartheid policies in the occupied West Bank.

A follower of Meir Kahane, an American-born Jewish supremacist, Ben Gvir has been convicted by Israeli courts of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organisation.

Earlier this month, Ben Gvir called on Israeli forces to kill “30 or 40” people in Gaza every night. He said some people there were “not worthy of life” and “not even people”.

When previously asked whether chanting “Death to Arabs” was morally wrong, Ben Gvir answered: “No. I don’t think so.”

His other “achievements” include introducing policies in Israeli prisons that human rights groups say amount to the starvation and torture of Palestinians.

item.description:
Israel to expel Palestinians in Gaza over kites flown by children

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Fri, 08/28/2026 - 12:59
Defence minister Israel Katz vows ‘severe response’ to balloons and kites that drift into Israel
A displaced Palestinian man helps a child to fly a kite near the border with Egypt in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip on 28 March 2024 (Said Khatib/AFP)
Off

The Israeli government has instructed its military to expel Palestinians from areas of the Gaza Strip where children are flying kites and releasing balloons, Israel’s Channel 13 reported on Thursday.

According to the report, Israeli defence minister Israel Katz told army chief Eyal Zamir and other senior military officials that “the ultimatum we issued following the launching of balloons and kites from the Gaza Strip towards Negev communities [in southern Israel] has expired”.

“Every launching of balloons and kites from Gaza towards southern communities will be met with a severe response,” Katz said during a meeting with the military’s top command.

From Israel’s perspective, Katz reportedly said, “every launch is an act of terrorism”, referring to kites and balloons that the Israeli army itself deemed a week ago to pose no danger to Israeli civilians.

“From now on, every launch will be met with a forceful response against those responsible, the organisers and the perpetrators,” Katz said, adding that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had ordered the new measure.

The Israeli military, Katz said, “will act with all necessary means, including evacuating the population from an area or neighbourhood from which launches are carried out, in order to deal with the centres of terrorism”.

Katz added that Israel would not allow Hamas or any other group to threaten Israeli communities near the Gaza Strip.

“Whoever does so will pay a heavy price,” he said.

Public demand for assassinations

In recent months, Israeli media have reported on kites being flown from the Gaza Strip, including an increase in the number of Palestinian kites crossing into Israel.

The newspaper Israel Hayom reported on Thursday that Israel’s security establishment sees Hamas as responsible for the increase, claiming the group is acting out of frustration over Israel’s deadly attacks on the besieged enclave.

Last week, Haaretz reported that four kites had been found in communities along the Gaza-Israel boundary, prompting residents to demand a military response. 

“This is how it started before 7 October,” one Israeli local community said last week, adding that it “will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security”.

Ori Epstein, head of the Sha’ar HaNegev Regional Council, said on Sunday that “a kite that crosses into Israeli territory is an incident that requires a response”.

For Gaza's orphans, the safety of childhood vanished with their parents
Read More »

“When there’s no response,” the Israeli local politician added, “the message that gets conveyed to the other side is that it’s allowed to continue.”

According to Channel 13, the Israeli military has responded to the public demands, with Zamir ordering an increase in targeted assassinations across the Gaza Strip earlier this week.

“Israel will not allow Hamas or any other party in the Gaza Strip to return to threatening our communities and undermining our citizens’ sense of security,” Netanyahu said on Monday after meeting Zamir.

The Israeli prime minister warned Hamas that if the kite launches did not stop, the military would strike “those responsible for the launches and will evacuate the population from areas from which kites, drones and balloons are launched”.

As Israeli threats over kites crossing into Israel increased, local non-governmental organisations in Gaza, in coordination with Hamas, urged parents to stop their children from flying kites.

“We are working tirelessly on the ground and doing everything possible to stop this practice,” the organisations said in a public statement, adding that they wanted to protect the lives of innocent children.

While Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip this week, killing Palestinian civilians, senior Hamas official Basem Naim commented on the Israeli threats over what Israel has described as “kite terrorism”.

“In a surreal paradox, a nuclear state that practises terrorism daily, charged with committing genocide in Gaza, mobilises and issues orders to deal forcefully with paper kites coming out of Gaza,” Naim said, stressing that children were flying the kites.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Britain's 'small boats' obsession misses the point on migration
item.description:
Britain's 'small boats' obsession misses the point on migration

Submitted by Barry Malone on Mon, 08/24/2026 - 11:53
Almost a month after the cynical weaponisation of Ceuta, racist scaremongering has kept its place at the top of the agenda
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks with interim Chief Coastguard and Border Security Commander as they stand by a recovered boat used by migrants crossing the English Channel, in Dover, on 2 August 2026 (AFP)
On

For a while there, it seemed like they’d stopped talking about it.

Andy Burnham had become prime minister and hit the ground running with a series of small but respectable measures aimed at alleviating what, for most people, is the most pressing problem in Britain: the cost of living. 

At the same time, Nigel Farage, leader of the hard-right Reform UK, had become a joke, running against a comedian with a bin on his head in a pointless by-election.

More seriously, behind the smokescreen that farce was intended to create, Farage had found himself at the centre of scandal after scandal, including a parliamentary standards watchdog inquiry into a series of “gifts” he had received like £5m ($6.8m) from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

For the first time, the swaggering marionette of the super-rich was looking vulnerable, with Burnham already pulling ahead of him in the polls.

Then Ceuta happened. An estimated 70,000 Moroccans entered the Spanish enclave in North Africa via sea and land, with at least 141 dying in the attempt.

Reform saw their chance, and before you could say "Ceuta is more than 1,000 miles from the UK", party spokesman Zia Yusuf was on a plane.

That Yusuf arrived in Ceuta as most people had gone back to Morocco didn't stop him from scaremongering on social media and in an interview with the Reform-adjacent GB News. He spoke darkly of "marauding migrants" despite only finding a few dozen men to film, one group eating biscuits as they happily spoke to him.

Hearing the dog whistle loud and clear, Reform supporters and other far-right elements in Britain, poured their ever-present Islamophobia out on social media, the so-called storming of Europe by Moroccans becoming a storm of Muslims.

But here's the thing: for all the absurdity of Reform's claims that the United Kingdom was about to be invaded because of an incident in North Africa - partly geopolitical in nature - that led to exactly zero people making it to mainland Spain, it worked.

Propaganda works

A day after Yusuf's grandstanding and acres of coverage in the reactionary media, Burnham showed up in Dover, where most asylum seekers crossing the English Channel from France to Britain arrive, pledging that he would be "relentless" in stopping the dreaded "small boats".

He even stood looking gravely at an empty dinghy put on display for him.

Elon Musk, UK far right, and Islamophobia: Why Humza Yousaf is sounding the alarm
Read More »

The images of the prime minister on the cliffs overlooking the Channel told us one thing clearly: Reform was framing the national conversation again.

And more than three weeks after Ceuta, the headlines continue.

The crossing of a larger-than-usual boat this month was splashed across the front pages, and Burnham was heckled in Ilkeston, a town in the Midlands, as he began a "listening tour" of the country, when a man shouted: "Any ideas how we're going to stop the boats?"

Giving an interview on migration to GB News didn't stop the channel from running a weak "exclusive" that found more people had arrived by boat in Burnham's first three weeks in office than in Starmer's. 

And, in a telling statistic last week, a Sky News/YouGov poll found that 40 percent of Britons incorrectly believed small boat crossings had gone up this year, despite Home Office statistics showing they were down 43 percent from last year, putting them at their lowest level since 2021.

It's clear that the far-right propaganda works, and time and time again the government and the media walk right into the trap.

If Burnham could resist kneejerk reactions due to Labour's fear of Reform and plant his feet on dealing with the cost of living, he could be onto a winner.

An Ipsos poll last month found that a staggering 76 percent of people in the UK were concerned about the impact of the rising cost of living on them personally over the next six months.

To be fair, Burnham also said that Britain should "offer support for people who genuinely need it" and that safe routes for asylum seekers should be created "because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs".

That may have pleased the centrist dads who are all in on the affable northerner, but those words are nothing new. Safe routes and smuggler crackdowns have been promised by a series of former prime ministers, from Boris Johnson to Starmer.

'Survival strategy'

The truth is that Britain is having the wrong conversation about migration. The relentless talk of enforcing the borders, smashing the trafficking networks and seeing off the "threat" of "migrants" misses the point entirely.

By the time you try to stop people in the Channel, it's already too late.

Britain is having the wrong conversation about migration. The relentless talk of enforcing the borders, smashing the trafficking networks and seeing off the "threat" of "migrants" misses the point entirely

It is clear to anyone with a conscience and a sense of humanity that desperate people fleeing war and oppression should not have to undertake the most perilous of journeys to exercise their right to claim asylum in a safe country.

Nobody wants people to drown, and of course the cold-blooded traffickers who see human beings as commodities should be stopped.

They are not the problem, though. They are a symptom that only exists because the immigration policies of European governments, including Britain's, create an environment in which they can thrive. Stop one gang and another appears.

Traffickers, though they may provide a convenient bogeyman, are not the first link in the chain that ends with desperate people crossing the English Channel. 

It begins in Syria, in Afghanistan, Sudan and Somalia. It begins in other places where people have no choice but to flee.

That the West destabilised many of the countries and regions from which frightened people have escaped over the last two decades doesn't appear to matter in a political environment that demands leaders be "tough on immigration".

As highlighted by Eric Reidy, migration and special coverage editor for The New Humanitarian, in the wake of what happened in Ceuta, human beings have always migrated to safety, long before our current borders existed.

"It is a fundamental human survival strategy and adaptation," he said.

That's an important point. People will always flee from danger; all of us would, which is why the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol exist.

Under it, recognising that people often have no other option, governments cannot punish asylum seekers for entering irregularly or without proper authorisation.

Britain is not only a signatory; it helped draft it.

Perhaps those involved in its initial conception as a mechanism to ensure safe havens for Europeans didn't foresee that it would eventually apply to people all over the world; people who have been forced out of their homes, often leaving full and happy lives behind.

But if it was good enough for white people, it's good enough for everyone else.

Humane response

There are clear things European governments could do to stop people setting out on perilous journeys during which they often die or are kidnapped by gangs and tortured while ransoms are demanded from their families at home. 

Britain helped create the refugees it now wants to keep out
Read More »

Very few people really want to take that risk – they do it because they have to. Given that, and given that the vast majority of people from war-torn countries take refuge in neighbouring countries hoping to go home soon, how about not cutting the development aid needed to ensure they have adequate food, shelter and education for their children there?

How about responding to the desperate pleas of the UN refugee agency?

As British-Somali poet Warsan Shire wrote in her poem "Home": "No one puts their children in a boat unless the water is safer than the land."

And Burnham is right. Safe routes are also desperately needed.

They are key to providing the sanctuary that everyone deserves and, though the rights of asylum seekers must always be the main consideration, they would provide the added benefit of neutralising the weaponisation of small boats.

But Burnham must, unlike other prime ministers, be clear on what safe routes will actually mean, because in recent years, only Ukrainians and Afghans have been granted them.

The government cannot be allowed to crack down harshly on irregular asylum seekers while simultaneously pledging to introduce safe routes in such a febrile political environment. Burnham and his home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, should develop the safe routes first – that is the only humane response.

It's time to stop deciding immigration and asylum policies based on political expediency. It's time to see asylum seekers as people, not pawns, and it's time to remember that Europeans were refugees once and could be again.

Taking in refugees isn't supposed to be easy. It's supposed to be right.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Cairo accused of ‘punishment by proxy’ after British-Egyptian woman arrested over sister's activism
item.description:
Cairo accused of ‘punishment by proxy’ after British-Egyptian woman arrested over sister's activism

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Fri, 08/28/2026 - 14:47
Lawyers say Egypt detained Eman el-Shazly to pressure her UK-based sister into ending her criticism of President Sisi
An Egyptian detention facility pictured in 2022 (Khaled Desouki/AFP)
Off

There is mounting alarm over the treatment of a British-Egyptian woman detained in Egypt on what her lawyers say are politically motivated charges intended to silence her sister.

Egyptian security personnel detained Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old mother of four from Birmingham, while she was visiting Egypt on 16 August.

Her lawyer said the authorities arrested her to intimidate the family and pressure her sister, Mona el-Shazly, into ending her criticism of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s government.

Mona runs a UK-based YouTube channel with 130,000 subscribers and remains active on X.

Much of her work focuses on corruption inside Egypt’s security services and public utilities, sectors in which the country’s secretive and powerful military has extensive business interests.

Eman’s lawyer said there were “compelling grounds” to conclude that the authorities detained her because of her sister’s political speech.

Her brothers, Hassan and Eid, previously spent nearly three years in pretrial detention on accusations routinely deployed against the Sisi government’s opponents, including “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

Families of Egyptian political prisoners launch UK advocacy group
Read More »

Egyptian authorities rearrested them in May.

The UK Foreign Office told the family that Egypt was holding Eman at the 10th of Ramadan Rehabilitation Centre and had placed her in the same case as her brothers.

Eman travelled to Egypt about two months before her arrest to care for her elderly and unwell mother.

On 18 August, Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution ordered her detention for 15 days pending further investigation.

She now faces the prospect of confinement in Egypt’s notoriously abusive prison system, where rights groups have documented extensive torture, medical neglect and degrading treatment.

The Sisi government has repeatedly targeted the relatives of critics living abroad, using their families as leverage to silence opposition beyond Egypt’s borders.

Request to stop criticism

Mona told The Guardian that relatives had asked her to remove her videos and stop her activism, but she refused.

“I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents," she said.

"It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing."

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has launched a fundraising campaign to cover the family’s mounting legal costs.

He said they remained “deeply concerned about her safety and wellbeing”.

The British government acknowledged earlier this year that Egypt regularly used “punishment by proxy” against critics living abroad.

Human Rights Watch has also documented the regime’s escalating use of relatives to intimidate dissidents.

British officials have requested consular access to Eman, but Egyptian authorities have yet to grant it.
